blocks.text: **Booting** is the startup procedure that prepares a computer for use. It wakes up the essential hardware and loads the operating-system **kernel** and the components it needs into **RAM**. The goal is simple: get the operating system ready so that it can manage the computer.

blocks.title: Key terms
rows: Startup procedure that initialises hardware and loads the OS kernel into RAM
Make the operating system ready to manage the computer
The core part of the operating system

blocks.title: A typical boot sequence
items: Firmware picks a boot device or entry
Loads the OS kernel into RAM

blocks.title: The sequence in words
items: Startup is triggered by the power button or a restart request.
BIOS or UEFI firmware begins to execute and initialises the hardware.
The firmware selects a boot device or startup entry.
The boot loader loads the OS kernel into RAM and hands control to it.
The OS initialises drivers, services and other system components.
The login screen or the desktop appears.

sections.title: Who starts first? Memory during boot

blocks.title: Order of loading (last loaded on top)
items: Word, Paint, browser - loaded after the OS
Kernel and system components in RAM
Loads the kernel and passes control

blocks.title: Where things live during boot
rows: Stored in non-volatile motherboard memory, usually flash
Normally stores the installed operating system
Holds the kernel and the active OS components

blocks.title: Textbook shorthand
blocks.text: Exam books say: **BIOS is in ROM** and the **operating system is loaded into RAM**. Firmware executes before the boot loader and the OS, and the OS is loaded before ordinary applications such as Word, Paint or a browser.

blocks.title: Memory trick
blocks.text: Order of startup: **F**irmware, **B**oot loader, **O**perating system, **A**pps - think 'Fast Boot Opens Apps'.

rows: Starting a computer from a powered-off state
Restarting a computer that is already running, without manually switching off its power
Pressing the power button after shutdown
Basic exam texts call it faster; real speed depends on hardware and startup features

blocks.title: Do not mix up
blocks.text: A cold boot does **not** mean only the first-ever startup of a new machine. Every start from the OFF state is a cold boot. Remember: **OFF to ON = cold boot, Restart = warm boot**.

blocks.title: Memory trick
blocks.text: Cold = the machine is cold (switched off). Warm = the machine is still warm (already running).

sections.title: Firmware: BIOS, UEFI, POST and CMOS

blocks.title: Full forms and meanings
rows: **Basic Input/Output System** - firmware that initialises hardware and begins startup
**Unified Extensible Firmware Interface** - the modern firmware interface that replaces legacy BIOS
**Power-On Self-Test** - firmware routines that check essential hardware such as memory and other devices; the exact checks vary
**EFI System Partition** - stores the UEFI startup files
Battery-backed memory in which traditional PCs kept BIOS settings
Non-volatile memory where modern firmware may keep its settings

blocks.title: More details
items: BIOS is traditionally described as stored in **ROM**; modern firmware commonly uses rewritable **flash memory**.
The EFI System Partition normally uses the **FAT32** file system on fixed disks; other partitions need not be FAT32.
Firmware **code** and firmware **settings** are different things - the code is in flash, the settings were kept in CMOS (older PCs) or NVRAM (modern ones).

blocks.title: POST is not a device
blocks.text: POST belongs to the **firmware**. It is not a separate hardware device. It runs the initial hardware checks right after the firmware starts.

sections.title: Boot loader, GRUB, dual boot and MBR

blocks.title: Startup tools
rows: Startup program that loads the operating-system kernel and transfers control to it
The small program that starts the OS-loading process
**GRand Unified Bootloader** - widely used with Linux; can show a menu to select an operating system
Two operating systems installed on one computer; the user chooses which one to start
**Master Boot Record** - a disk structure that traditionally holds initial boot code and partition information
Firmware feature that shortens startup by skipping or reducing some initialisation work

blocks.title: Dual boot with GRUB
items: Starts and finds the boot loader

blocks.text: **GRUB = Linux boot loader.** A boot loader loads the kernel; it is not the operating system itself.

blocks.title: Advanced boot options
rows: Starts Windows with a limited set of essential files, drivers and services; useful to diagnose startup and software problems
Safe Mode plus the network components
Safe Mode that opens a command prompt instead of the normal desktop

blocks.title: Ctrl + Alt + Delete
blocks.text: On older PCs this key combination was historically associated with a **warm reboot**. In modern Windows it normally opens the **security screen** and does not directly restart the PC.

items: Safe Mode loads **limited drivers** - helpful when a faulty driver or software stops normal startup.
The advanced boot menu lets you choose how Windows starts.

blocks.text: '**Random booting**' is an informal phrase for sudden or repeated unexpected restarts. It is a **fault symptom**, not a standard boot type like cold or warm boot.

blocks.title: Boot failure
blocks.text: A **boot failure** means the startup cannot finish. Corrupted startup files can also prevent the computer from completing startup.

**Unicode** assigns a **code point** to characters from many writing systems. It represents letters, numbers, punctuation, symbols and other text elements consistently, and is used by operating systems, browsers, search engines and applications.

blocks.title: What Unicode is not
blocks.text: Unicode is a **character-encoding standard**, not a font and not a keyboard layout. 'Universal character-encoding standard' describes its purpose - Unicode is **not an acronym**.

blocks.title: Unicode history
items: Joe Becker, Lee Collins and Mark Davis, associated with Xerox and Apple

blocks.text: The **Unicode Consortium** maintains the standard.

sections.title: UTF forms, encodings, ASCII and EBCDIC

blocks.text: **UTF** stands for **Unicode Transformation Format**. An **encoding** represents text as numeric values stored as binary data. Unicode has three main encoding forms, and all of them represent the same Unicode repertoire.

blocks.title: From code point to what you see
items: Unicode number that identifies the character
The abstract letter or symbol (Latin capital A)
Drawn by the font you use

blocks.title: Important distinctions
blocks.text: Unicode has **no single fixed bit length** - 8, 16 and 32 are code-unit sizes of its forms. One visible symbol can contain several code points. A **font supplies glyph shapes**; **Unicode identifies characters**.

**ASCII** (American Standard Code for Information Interchange) is a common numeric code for exchanging text between computers and communication equipment. It represents English letters, digits, punctuation, spaces and control functions.

blocks.title: ASCII milestones
items: IBM engineer **Bob Bemer** contributed a proposal for a common character code
First ASCII standard published under the American Standards Association (ASA)

blocks.text: ASA was a predecessor of today's **ANSI** - American National Standards Institute.

blocks.title: Standard ASCII vs Extended ASCII
rows: Control positions 0-31 and 127; printable positions 32-126 (including space)
Upper-half values depend on the code page

blocks.title: Extended ASCII is not one table
blocks.text: 'Extended ASCII' means **several ASCII-based 8-bit code pages**, not one universal table. Also remember that 128-255 is only the upper half - the complete 8-bit range is 0-255.

blocks.title: ASCII vs Unicode
rows: UTF-8 preserves the same byte values for ASCII characters

blocks.title: The 32 rule
blocks.text: Each lowercase ASCII letter is **32 greater** than its uppercase partner (97 - 65 = 32 and 122 - 90 = 32). Uppercase to lowercase: **add 32**. Lowercase to uppercase: **subtract 32**.
The +32 / -32 rule works only for corresponding **ASCII letters**, not for all Unicode scripts.

revision: Booting = startup procedure; 'boot' comes from bootstrap; it loads the OS kernel into RAM.
Boot order: power on, BIOS/UEFI, POST, boot device selection, boot loader, OS, login screen.
Firmware runs first, then the boot loader, then the OS, and only then ordinary applications.
BIOS = Basic Input/Output System (textbook: in ROM); UEFI = Unified Extensible Firmware Interface (modern replacement).
POST = Power-On Self-Test, run by the firmware to check essential hardware.
Cold boot = starting from OFF; warm boot = restart while running (soft reboot).
GRUB = GRand Unified Bootloader, widely used with Linux; dual boot = two OS on one computer.
MBR = Master Boot Record; ESP (EFI System Partition) holds UEFI files, normally FAT32.
Safe Mode starts Windows with limited drivers and services for diagnosing problems.
Ctrl+Alt+Delete opens the security screen in modern Windows; it does not directly restart the PC.
'Random booting' is a fault symptom (bad RAM, overheating, power, malware, drivers), not a boot type.
Unicode: work began 1987, Consortium incorporated 3 Jan 1991, Unicode 1.0.0 in October 1991.
UTF-8 uses 1-4 bytes, UTF-16 uses 2 or 4 bytes, UTF-32 uses 4 bytes; Unicode is not an acronym.
ASCII = 7 bits, 128 values, range 0-127; extended ASCII = 8 bits, 256 values, range 0-255.
ASCII values: 0-9 = 48-57, A-Z = 65-90, a-z = 97-122; lowercase = uppercase + 32; space = 32.
